classification.difficultyReason: Identify the high outlier at low study time and infer that removing its pull on the left end makes the positive fitted line steeper.

content.prompt: A survey collected data on hours studying and score on quiz.

spec.description: Rectangular unit grid, labelled axes with x and y at arrowheads, thirteen circular data markers and a supplied rising line of best fit. Non-outlier coordinates and line endpoints are reconstructed approximately from the source image.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal axis: hours of study, ticks 1–8. Vertical axis: score on quiz, ticks 1–10. Outlier (0.3,10). Other plotted points approximately (0.6,1), (1,3), (1.7,3), (2.2,5), (2.8,5), (3.2,6), (3.8,7), (4.4,10), (4.5,8), (5,9), (5.2,10), (5.6,10). Supplied line approximately from (0,3.1) to (6.4,10.5).
spec.answerVisibility: The supplied line and every data point are permanent givens. No circle or supplied answer appears in the question diagram.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Identify the outlier. Circle the data point.

answer.worked: Circle $(0.3,10)$. This point lies well above the rising pattern formed by the other data points.

spec.description: Circle around the outlier in the exact coordinate frame and bounding box of the question graph.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the outlier were removed, what would happen to the gradient of the line of best fit? Would it be steeper or less steep?

answer.short: The gradient becomes more positive; the line becomes steeper.
answer.worked: The high score at only $0.3$ hours pulls the left end of the line upwards, making its positive gradient smaller. Removing this outlier makes the gradient more positive, so the line becomes steeper.
